title: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
summary: Certificates are not only for signing and encryption; when a certificate authority issues one that maps to a user or machine identity, that certificate becomes a credential. An adversary can take it in several ways. A stolen certificate may be pulled from encrypted storage in the registry, from a certificate file left in the wrong place, or directly from the Windows certificate store through crypto interfaces. Where enrolment rights allow it, an attacker with a foothold can also request a certificate from the enterprise authority and control the subject alternative name or extended key usage values written into it. With access to a certificate authority's private key, an attacker can forge certificates for any identity in the domain, which is the idea behind the so-called golden certificate. The value to the attacker is durability: a certificate keeps working while it is valid, even after a password reset. Detection focuses on enrolment events, unusual templates, requests with mismatched names, and certificate based sign-ins from unexpected hosts.

beginner.definition: A digital certificate is a signed file that proves an identity, much like a passport. Some systems accept a certificate instead of a password. If an attacker steals or fakes one, they can log in as somebody else without knowing that person's password.
beginner.whyItMatters: Passwords can be changed quickly after an incident. A stolen certificate cannot, so the attacker keeps access for as long as it stays valid. A forged certificate can copy any account in the company, including administrator accounts. Because the certificate looks genuine, the login may raise no alarm at all. This makes your certificate authority one of the most valuable systems you own.
howItWorks: The attacker gains a foothold on a machine or an account inside the network.
They search for certificate files, stored keys, or the local certificate store.
Alternatively they request a new certificate from the company authority using valid enrolment rights.
They may change the name fields so the certificate claims a more powerful identity.
They use the certificate to sign in to services, which accept it as proof of identity.
Access continues while the certificate is valid, even if the real user changes the password.
beginner.example: Think about a hospital where staff wear photo badges to open locked wards. A stolen password is like a forgotten door code, and the hospital can change that code the same day. A stolen badge is different. It still opens the ward, because the lock trusts the badge and not the person. Now imagine someone found the machine that prints badges and made one with a doctor's name on it. Every door would open for them. Certificates used as login credentials work this way. The system trusts the certificate. A stolen or forged one keeps working until it expires or the issuer cancels it.
takeaways: Treat authentication certificates as credentials, not just as encryption files.
Protect certificate authority private keys as your most sensitive assets.
Watch enrolment logs for requests with unusual names, templates, or requesters.

objectives: Explain how a certificate can act as a login credential.
Describe the ways an attacker steals a certificate from a Windows system.
Explain what a forged certificate allows and why it survives a password reset.
Identify the events that record certificate enrolment and issuance.
Outline the controls that limit who may request a certificate.
